## Twist card: add an excess {.excess-slide}

::: {.keyphrase}
New rule: customers now pay the **first $200** of any claim themselves.
:::

::: {.quiz}
::: {.q}
**1. When someone claims, how much does your company pay now?**

::: {.fragment .a}
$600 − $200 = **$400**.
:::
:::
::: {.q}
**2. About 1 in 6 customers claims. What does that cost you per customer?**

::: {.fragment .a}
$400 ÷ 6 ≈ **$67** each (it was $100).
:::
:::
::: {.q}
**3. Should your premium go up or down?**

::: {.fragment .a}
Down, by about $33. That's why a policy with a higher excess is cheaper.
:::
:::
::: {.q}
**4. Why might customers with an excess break fewer phones?**

::: {.fragment .a}
They lose $200 when it happens, so they're more careful. Fewer claims, cheaper again.
:::
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
About 5 min, straight after the game. Optional: skip if short of time. Ask each question, give teams 30 seconds, take an answer, then reveal.

Easier alternatives if you want a different twist:

- Repair costs go up: a new phone costs $900 to fix. New fair premium? $900 ÷ 6 = $150.
- Clumsy class: a 1 or a 2 is now a claim. Chance 2 in 6, fair premium $600 × 2/6 = $200.

For a strong maths class, follow with the next slide (how sure do you want to be?).
:::
